text: Amcor plc, originally incorporated as Arctic Jersey Limited under the laws of the Bailiwick of Jersey in July 2018 to facilitate its merger with Bemis Company, Inc., was renamed Amcor plc and became a public limited company under the same jurisdiction on October 10, 2018. On June 11, 2019, Amcor completed the acquisition of Bemis Company, Inc. pursuant to a definitive merger agreement dated August 6, 2018, under which Bemis shareholders received 5.1 Amcor shares for each Bemis share, and Amcor shareholders received one Amcor CHESS Depositary Instrument (CDI) for each Amcor Limited share outstanding. Following the transaction, Amcor shares were registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol "AMCR," while CDIs were traded on the Australian Securities Exchange under the symbol "AMC." Amcor Limited shares were delisted from the ASX, and Bemis shares were delisted from the NYSE. The Company’s business strategy centers on a focused portfolio of strong businesses in flexible and rigid packaging, specialty cartons, and closures, driven by a focus on primary packaging for fast-moving consumer goods, favorable industry structures, attractive relative growth, and multiple competitive advantages. This strategy is supported by differentiated capabilities known as "The Amcor Way," including Talent, Commercial Excellence, Operational Leadership, Innovation, and Cash and Capital Discipline. The Company operates two reporting segments under ASC 280: Flexibles and Rigid Packaging. As of June 30, 2020, the Flexibles Segment, which employs approximately 40,000 people across 181 manufacturing facilities in 39 countries, accounted for about 78% of consolidated net sales, while the Rigid Packaging Segment, employing approximately 6,000 people at 50 facilities in 11 countries, accounted for about 22% of consolidated net sales. Sales are primarily conducted through a direct sales force with offices and plants in Europe, North America, Latin America, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific region, and no single customer accounted for more than 10% of consolidated net sales in fiscal year 2020; sales to PepsiCo and its subsidiaries were approximately 11.1% and 11.0% in fiscal years 2019 and 2018, respectively, with arrangements aggregated across multiple contracts. The Company competes in highly competitive markets based on service, innovation, quality, and price, with key competitors including AptarGroup, Inc., Ball Corporation, Berry Global Group, Inc., CCL Industries Inc., Crown Holdings, Inc., Graphic Packaging Holding Company, Huhtamaki Oyj, International Paper Company, Mayr-Melnhof Karton AG, O-I Glass, Inc., Sealed Air Corporation, Silgan Holdings Inc., Sonoco Products Company, WestRock Company, and various privately held companies. The Company maintains inventory levels to balance favorable raw material pricing with timely order fulfillment and does not rely on any single supplier for major raw materials such as polymer resins and films, paper, inks, adhesives, aluminum, and chemicals, which are sourced globally. While raw material availability is currently stable, pricing may fluctuate. Amcor owns or licenses U.S. and international patents, trademarks, and trade secrets related to its products, processes, and equipment, which provide a competitive advantage, though the loss of any single patent or license would not have a material adverse effect on overall operations. The Company believes primary packaging remains essential for protecting and preserving food and healthcare products and is subject to environmental, health, and safety laws and regulations.

While temporary industry-wide shortages of raw materials may occur, the company expects to continue managing raw material supplies effectively without significant supply interruptions. Currently, raw materials are readily available, though pricing may fluctuate. The company owns or licenses a number of United States and international patents and patent applications related to its products, manufacturing processes, and equipment, and holds trademarks and trademark registrations in the United States and other countries. Certain technology and processes are maintained as trade secrets. Collectively, these intellectual property rights provide a competitive advantage, but the loss of any single patent or license would not have a material adverse effect on overall results of operations or those of its reporting segments. Patents, patent applications, and license agreements will expire or terminate over time due to their terms or by operation of law. Amcor believes packaging plays a vital role in protecting and preserving food and healthcare products, extending shelf life, reducing product loss, and lowering carbon footprint and waste. Consumers prefer cost-effective, convenient, and easy-to-use packaging with end-of-life solutions to reduce waste. Amcor is committed to responsible packaging and, in January 2018, became the first global packaging company to pledge to develop all of its packaging to be recyclable or reusable by 2025, to significantly increase the use of recycled materials, and to collaborate with others to improve global recycling of packaging. The company is recognized for its innovation, holding thousands of active patents, and collaborates with customers, suppliers, and innovators to deliver industry-leading solutions and to enhance waste collection, sorting, and recycling infrastructure while informing consumers about the environmental impact of packaging. Amcor is uniquely positioned to lead in developing more sustainable and environmentally friendly packaging, which is seen as a key growth opportunity. The company’s operations and real property are subject to broad environmental laws and regulations across multiple jurisdictions, covering discharges of materials, waste handling and disposal, and cleanup of contaminated soil and groundwater. The company believes it is in substantial compliance with these regulations through its Environmental, Health, and Safety Management System and regular audits, though it cannot predict with certainty whether it may incur material liability for noncompliance due to contamination at former or current sites (including contamination from prior owners or operators) or off-site disposal of regulated materials. These laws and regulations are constantly evolving, and the company cannot always anticipate changes. Key risk factors include changes in consumer demand, where shifts in preferences for products or packaging formats may reduce demand for certain products or lead to obsolescence, despite mitigation strategies; key customer and customer consolidation risks, where loss of key customers or reduced production requirements could significantly impact sales and profitability, with sales to the largest customer accounting for approximately 11% of total net sales in fiscal years 2019 and 2018, and no single customer exceeding 10% of net sales in 2020 or any other period; competition in highly competitive geographies and end-use areas, where competitors may develop disruptive technologies or innovations that could harm competitiveness; challenges in expanding current business through organic growth or acquisitions, due to market saturation, changing customer plans, or difficulty identifying and acquiring suitable targets, especially given increased price multiples and competition for targets; integration challenges from acquisitions, including difficulties in merging business processes, systems, and cultures, and potential disruptions to operations, with the Bemis acquisition expected to generate approximately $180 million in pre-tax annual net cost synergies by the end of the third year from procurement, manufacturing, and general and administrative efficiencies, though full realization is not guaranteed; and intellectual property risks, where third parties could obtain information, independently develop similar technologies, or breach non-disclosure agreements, particularly in emerging markets where intellectual property protection is less robust, potentially reducing competitive advantages, causing lost sales, or requiring costly litigation or licensing; operational risks, including the impact of global health outbreaks such as the 2019 Novel Coronavirus (COVID-19), which has led to volatility in customer order patterns, temporary facility or supplier shutdowns, and a $25.6 million impairment of an equity method investment in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2020 due to pandemic-related market declines.

To contain the virus, governments have implemented measures such as travel bans, gathering limitations, quarantines, shelter-in-place orders, and business shutdowns. These business shutdowns typically exclude essential services and critical infrastructure supporting them. The company has experienced minimal operational disruptions because it is largely considered to provide essential services. However, customer order patterns have been volatile in the second half of fiscal year 2020, and such volatility could persist in the future. In the fourth quarter, an equity method investment was impaired by $25.6 million, partly due to general market declines linked to the pandemic. See Note 7, "Equity Method Investments," in the notes to consolidated financial statements for further details. The coronavirus has significantly impacted and may further impact the economies and financial markets of affected countries, negatively affecting economic growth, capital market functioning, foreign currency exchange rates, and interest rates. It may result in prolonged economic downturns, such as increased unemployment, reduced capital spending, business shutdowns, or recessions, which could reduce demand for customers’ products. Despite efforts to manage these impacts, the extent to which the coronavirus or other outbreaks affect the company’s operations—including its ability to secure financing at attractive rates—is unknown and could be material. Global economic challenges, including high unemployment in certain operating regions, low economic growth, and difficulties managing rising debt and economic volatility, have negatively impacted and may continue to negatively impact the company’s operations and financial results. Demand for the company’s products and services depends on consumer demand for packaged food, beverage, healthcare, personal care, agribusiness, industrial, and other consumer goods. General economic downturns in key geographic regions and globally can adversely affect the company’s operations and financial results. The current global economic challenges, including relatively high unemployment, low growth, and difficulties with rising debt and volatility in certain economies, are likely to continue exerting pressure on the global economy and the company’s business. The COVID-19 pandemic has increased global economic volatility. During challenging economic conditions, customers may delay, reduce, or cancel purchases, delay payments, or fail to pay, suppliers may struggle to fulfill orders, and distributors may face difficulties delivering products, all of which could impair the company’s ability to meet customer demands and result in lost business. Weakened global economic conditions may also lead to unfavorable changes in product pricing, product mix, and lower profit margins. All of these factors could adversely affect the company’s business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations, which effect may be material. Political uncertainty may also contribute to economic conditions in markets where the company operates. For example, the United Kingdom’s exit from the European Union has caused significant volatility in global financial markets and altered market behavior. Such political developments could disrupt markets served and tax jurisdictions, potentially leading to loss of customers, suppliers, and employees, and negatively impacting profitability. The company’s international operations expose it to various risks that could adversely affect its business and financial results. It operates globally, including in emerging markets. In fiscal year 2020, approximately 74% of sales revenue came from developed markets and 26% from emerging markets. The company expects to continue expanding, particularly in emerging markets. Managing global operations is complex due to substantial differences in cultural, political, and regulatory environments. Many countries where the company operates, including Argentina, Brazil, China, India, and other emerging markets, have underdeveloped or developing legal, regulatory, or political systems that are subject to dynamic change and civil unrest. The profitability of operations may be adversely impacted by: changes in fiscal or regulatory regimes; difficulties in interpreting or complying with local laws, including tax, labor, foreign investment, and foreign exchange control; nullification, modification, or renegotiation of, or difficulties in enforcing, contracts subject to local law; reversal of policies encouraging foreign investment or trade or relating to local agents or partners; pandemics such as COVID-19 affecting regions unequally; or changes in exchange rates and inflation, including hyperinflation, which may be worsened by the pandemic. Sustained legal, regulatory, or political instability in emerging markets could adversely affect the company’s business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations, which effect may be material. The international scope of operations includes limited sales to entities in countries subject to U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control, U.S. Department of State, Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and other national or supranational sanctions (collectively, “Sanctions”), and operations in countries periodically subject to Sanctions. This requires maintaining internal processes and controls. Failure to do so could result in employee breaches of laws and regulations, including those related to money laundering, corruption, export control, fraud, bribery, insider trading, antitrust, competition, and economic sanctions, due to lack of integrity or awareness. Any such breach could adversely affect financial condition and cause reputational damage, which effect may be material. Price fluctuations or shortages in raw materials, energy, and other inputs could adversely affect the business. As a packaging manufacturer, sales and profitability depend on the availability and cost of raw materials, labor, and other inputs, including energy. All raw materials are sourced from third parties, with primary inputs including polymer resins and films, inks and solvents, aluminum, and fiber-based carton board. Prices for these inputs are subject to substantial fluctuations due to changing economic conditions, pandemics (such as COVID-19), currency and commodity price fluctuations, resource availability, transportation costs, weather, natural disasters, political unrest, and other supply and demand factors. Increased costs can negatively affect business and financial results. Although the company uses strategies such as price adjustments with customers or increasing prices to offset input cost increases, there is no guarantee of anticipating or mitigating such movements, there may be delays in adjusting prices, and failure to do so could adversely affect business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations, which effect may be material. The company faces commercial risks, including operational disruptions such as mechanical or technology failures or forced closures due to pandemics (such as COVID-19), which could lead to production loss and increased costs; shortages in manufacturing inputs due to loss of key suppliers or their inability to supply; and risks related to development projects (such as cost overruns and delays). Many production and business locations are vulnerable to natural disasters, including earthquakes, snowstorms, hurricanes, forest fires, and flooding. Unplanned plant downtime at any facility would likely result in unabsorbed fixed costs that could negatively impact results of operations for the period. Supply shortages or disruptions in the supply chain—due to reliance on single suppliers or events such as the COVID-19 pandemic or natural disasters—could impair timely delivery of raw materials, equipment, and supplies, thereby affecting the ability to supply products to customers. Such disruptions could adversely affect business and financial results. In response to the pandemic, the company has implemented employee safety measures across all supply chain facilities, including proper hygiene, social distancing, and temporary screening, which are at a minimum compliant with local government regulations. These measures may not prevent the spread of COVID-19, and illness, travel restrictions, absenteeism, or other workforce disruptions could negatively impact supply chain, manufacturing, distribution, or other business activities. The insolvency or contractual default of any customer, supplier, or financial institution—such as banks or insurance providers—could significantly harm operations and financial condition. These risks are exacerbated during economic volatility (such as that caused by the pandemic), either globally or in specific geographies or industries. If a counterparty defaults on a payment, the company may be unable to collect the owed amount and may need to write it off. If a counterparty becomes insolvent or fails to meet obligations, the company may need to find a replacement or fulfill obligations itself, which would likely be more expensive. The occurrence of any such risk, including counterparty default, could adversely affect business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations, which effect may be material and result in a competitive disadvantage. A failure or disruption in information technology systems could disrupt operations, compromise customer, employee, vendor, and other data, and negatively affect business. The company relies on uninterrupted functioning of its information technology and control systems to manage operations and business functions, process, store, and report information, and interact with customers, vendors, and employees globally. Increasing reliance on cloud solutions requires different security measures, including technical network security improvements, organizational and governance changes, and alignment with third-party vendors on market standards. As with large systems, IT systems may be vulnerable to damage, disruption, information loss, or shutdown due to power outages, software or hardware failures, computer viruses, cyber-attacks, catastrophic events, telecommunications failures, user errors, unauthorized access, or malicious or accidental destruction or theft of information or functionality. The company maintains and accesses sensitive, confidential, or personal data subject to privacy and security laws and customer controls. Despite protective efforts, facilities and systems—including those of customers and third-party service providers—may be vulnerable to security breaches, misplaced or lost data, and user errors that could compromise such data. Information system damages, disruptions, shutdowns, or compromises could result in production downtimes, operational disruptions, transaction errors, loss of customers and business opportunities, violations of privacy laws, legal liability, regulatory fines or penalties, negative publicity, reputational damage, reimbursement or compensatory payments, and other costs, any of which could adversely affect business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations, which effect may be material and result in a competitive disadvantage. Although mitigation measures are in place, systems, networks, products, and services remain potentially vulnerable to advanced and persistent threats. The company’s continued success depends on its ability to identify, attract, motivate, train, and retain qualified personnel in key functions and geographic areas. Losing key employees could make it difficult to meet objectives. There is no assurance that the company will be able to recruit, train, assimilate, motivate, and retain future employees who meet cultural standards. The company is subject to costs and liabilities related to current and future environmental and health and safety laws and regulations that could adversely affect business. Compliance with environmental and health and safety laws, rules, and regulations in each country where it operates is required. Many products come into contact with food and beverages, so the company is also subject to local and international standards related to such products. Compliance requires significant financial and employee resources. Changes to such laws, regulations, and standards are regularly proposed, and some may directly or indirectly result in a material reduction in operating results. For example, increased legislation on plastic packaging litter or recycling may lead to bans or limitations on certain packaging formats or materials in some countries or regions. Increased regulation of emissions linked to climate change, including greenhouse gas (carbon) emissions, could increase operational costs due to compliance costs, higher fossil fuel inputs, and more expensive energy-intensive raw materials. However, the extent of such changes is uncertain, and the company cannot predict additional capital or operating expenses required for compliance. Federal, state, provincial, foreign, and local environmental requirements related to air, soil, and water quality, handling, discharge, storage, and disposal of substances, and climate change are significant factors in operations. Changes to such requirements generally increase operational costs. The company may face environmental liability for the costs of remediating contaminated soil or water at its owned, used, or operated facilities (including future acquisitions). Legal proceedings may result in fines, penalties, and mandated remediation programs requiring substantial, sometimes unplanned, capital expenditures. The effects of climate change and greenhouse gas emissions may adversely affect business. Numerous governmental bodies have introduced or are considering introducing regulatory changes to address climate change impacts, which, if implemented, could negatively affect operations or financial results. The company has incurred and may incur fines, penalties, legal costs related to environmental matters, and costs for damage to natural resources, lost property values, and toxic tort claims. Provisions are made when it is probable that liability exists. However, because the extent of potential environmental damage and the company’s liability is usually difficult to assess and may only be determined over a long period, actual liability may end up substantially higher than currently provisioned amounts. Additional charges could result, adversely affecting operating results and financial position, which may be material. The company is subject to the risk of labor disputes, which could adversely affect business. Although no significant labor disputes have occurred in recent years, there is no assurance that future disputes—including protests and strikes—will not arise, which could disrupt operations and negatively affect business and results of operations. Although relations with employees are currently good, there is no assurance that satisfactory working relationships will be maintained in the future. Financial risks include LIBOR-indexed borrowings and foreign exchange rate exposure. A substantial portion of the company’s borrowing capacity bears interest at a variable rate based on the London Interbank Offered Rate ("LIBOR"). In July 2017, the United Kingdom’s Financial Conduct Authority (“FCA”), which regulates LIBOR, announced its intention to phase out LIBOR by the end of 2021. The U.S. Federal Reserve, in coordination with the Alternative Reference Rates Committee—a steering committee of major U.S. financial institutions—is considering replacing LIBOR with the Secured Overnight Financing Rate ("SOFR"), a new index based on short-term repurchase agreements backed by Treasury securities. Some financing agreements include language to determine a replacement rate for LIBOR if needed. However, if LIBOR ceases to exist, the company may need to renegotiate financing agreements extending beyond 2021 that use LIBOR. The company is evaluating the potential impact of the transition from LIBOR, but cannot predict whether LIBOR will cease after 2021, whether SOFR will become widely accepted, or the impact of such a transition on business, financial condition, and results of operations. The company is exposed to foreign exchange rate risk, both transactional and translational. Transactional exposures arise from exchange rate fluctuations affecting costs (in currencies such as the U.S. dollar, Euro, or Latin American currencies) and sales proceeds. Translational exposures result from converting entity functional currencies to U.S. dollars for reporting purposes and may affect the reported value of assets and liabilities and income and expenses. In particular, translational exposure may be affected by movements in the exchange rate between the Euro and the Brazilian Real against the U.S. dollar. Exchange rates have varied in recent years and remain subject to further movement. Exchange rates between transactional currencies may change rapidly. For instance, the Mexican peso and the Brazilian Real have experienced such fluctuations.

In 2021, the company is evaluating whether the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) will become a widely accepted benchmark replacing LIBOR, and assessing the potential impact of such a transition on its business, financial condition, and results of operations. The company is exposed to foreign exchange rate risk, both transactional and translational, which could negatively affect its financial performance. Transactional exposures arise from fluctuations in exchange rates involving the U.S. dollar, Euro, and other currencies, including those in Latin America, impacting input costs and product sales proceeds. Translational exposures occur when converting entity functional currencies to U.S. dollars for reporting purposes and may affect the reported value of assets, liabilities, income, and expenses, particularly due to movements in the exchange rate between the Euro and the Brazilian Real. Exchange rates between transactional currencies can change rapidly, as seen in the Mexican peso and Brazilian Real, which have faced significant devaluation due to economic concerns, including the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The company has recognized foreign exchange losses related to Argentina’s currency devaluation and its designation as a highly inflationary economy under U.S. GAAP, as detailed in Note 2 of the financial statements. Continued currency devaluation could lead to a lag in passing through U.S. dollar-denominated input costs, adversely affecting margins and profitability, and exposing the company to future exchange rate fluctuations that could materially harm reported cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations. Increases in interest rates could raise borrowing costs and negatively impact results of operations, particularly affecting interest payments on variable-rate borrowings, as noted in Note 13 of the financial statements. A downgrade in the company’s credit rating could reduce access to the commercial paper market, increase borrowing costs or fees, or widen credit spreads when issuing debt, due to assessments by credit rating agencies based on financial performance, industry outlook, and global economic conditions. The company has a hedging policy to manage interest rate and foreign exchange risks, but failure to hedge effectively, under-hedging, or a default by a hedge provider could adversely affect business, cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations. The company identified two material weaknesses in internal controls during the transition from Australian Accounting Standards (AAS) to U.S. GAAP: a lack of accounting staff with U.S. GAAP experience and deficiencies in segregation of duties within key IT systems used for financial reporting. Failure to remediate these weaknesses or identify new ones could impair financial reporting accuracy, damage investor confidence, and negatively affect the trading price of common stock. Environmental, health, and safety regulations, especially those related to greenhouse gas emissions and climate change, could increase raw material, energy, and freight costs, restrict the use of certain materials, and require additional compliance costs, particularly in highly regulated markets like healthcare and food and beverage packaging. The company’s success depends on its ability to develop and introduce new products and maintain intellectual property rights through patents, trademarks, trade secrets, and licensing, but pending applications may not be approved, and competitors may challenge validity or scope, or develop non-infringing alternatives, potentially weakening its competitive position. Under English insolvency law, if a company enters administration or liquidation, the administrator or liquidator may apply to the court for an order—such as setting aside a transaction—to restore the position as if the company had not entered into a transaction at an "undervalue," defined under the UK Insolvency Act 1986, if the transaction occurred within two years of the onset of insolvency. A transaction is at an undervalue if the company makes a gift or receives consideration significantly below the value of what it gives. Courts generally will not intervene if the transaction was in good faith for business purposes and there were reasonable grounds to believe it would benefit the company. Additionally, if a "preference" is given within six months (or two years if to a connected person) of insolvency, the court may set it aside to restore the position as if the preference had not occurred. A preference occurs when a company does something that puts a creditor, surety, or guarantor in a better position during insolvency than they would have been otherwise. Courts will only make such orders if the company was insolvent at the time of the transaction or became insolvent as a result of it, and for preferences, the company must have been influenced by a desire to improve the beneficiary’s position in insolvency, though this is presumed if the beneficiary is a connected person. If a transaction is made at an undervalue with the purpose of putting assets beyond the reach or prejudicing the interests of creditors, the court may set it aside and protect the interests of "victims" of the transaction, with no statutory time limit for claims except relevant limitation periods, and the company need not be insolvent at the time of the transaction or in liquidation. Under Australian insolvency laws, a guarantee may not be enforceable if a court finds that the guarantor was insolvent at the time of providing the guarantee or became insolvent as a result, or if, upon application of a liquidator, winding up has begun within four years of the guarantee’s issuance and the guarantee is deemed an "uncommercial transaction" under the Australian Act, based on whether a reasonable person in the guarantor’s position would have issued it after considering the benefits, detriments, benefits to other parties, and other relevant facts. Under U.S. bankruptcy law and state fraudulent transfer laws, a guarantee may be voided or claims subordinated if the guarantor at the time of incurrence: (1) intended to hinder, delay, or defraud a creditor or received less than reasonably equivalent value or fair consideration; (2) was insolvent or rendered insolvent by the incurrence; (3) was engaged in a business or transaction with unreasonably small capital relative to its remaining assets; or (4) intended or believed it would incur debts beyond its ability to pay as they mature. Any payments under the guarantee may be voided and returned to the guarantor or to a creditor fund. Insolvency under fraudulent transfer laws generally means: (1) the sum of debts, including contingent liabilities, exceeds the fair saleable value of all assets; (2) the present fair saleable value of assets is less than the amount needed to pay existing debts as they mature; or (3) the guarantor cannot pay its debts as they become due. Under Jersey law, under Article 17 of the Bankruptcy (Désastre) (Jersey) Law 1990 and Article 176 of the Jersey Companies Law, the court may set aside a guarantee entered into at an undervalue if the company’s property is declared "en désastre" or undergoing creditors' winding up, with a five-year look-back period from the commencement of winding up or declaration. If the transaction is found to be at an undervalue, the court may restore the position as if it had not occurred. The Viscount of Jersey or liquidator must prove insolvency unless the beneficiary is a connected person, in which case there is a presumption of insolvency and the connected person must prove otherwise. Under Article 17A and Article 176A, the court may set aside a preference (including a guarantee) given to any person, with a 12-month look-back period. A guarantee constitutes a preference if it puts a creditor or guarantor in a better position during insolvency than they would have been otherwise. If the court finds such a preference, it has wide powers to restore the position. However, it must be shown that the company was influenced by a desire to produce the preferential effect; in proceedings, the Viscount or liquidator must prove insolvency and the desire to create the preference, unless the beneficiary is a connected person, in which case there is a presumption of such desire and the connected person must prove otherwise. In addition to statutory provisions, Jersey customary law, such as a Pauline action, may allow setting aside asset dispositions intended to defeat creditor claims. A Participant will not receive under the Pension Plan due to: (i) the limitations of Section 401(a)(17) of the Code, (ii) the limitations of Section 415 of the Code, and (iii) the fact that a Participant’s Employee Contributions into this Plan are not included as compensation for purposes of determining eligibility or benefit amounts. An Employer will continue to make Employer Make-Up Pension Contributions past the date when a Participant reaches age 60 or completes 5 years of service, whichever occurs first, to account for service after that date. For purposes of determining the amount of a Participant’s Employer Make-Up Pension Contribution each Plan Year, the Employer will base contributions on Compensation, the GAM 94 mortality table, and assumed Compensation increases of inflation plus 1.5%, provided that all actuarial assumptions may vary as the Committee determines advisable. The Employer will hypothetically assume that prior Employer Make-Up Pension Contributions on a Participant’s account are not included in the calculation of future contributions. A Participant shall not receive the entire amount of Employer Make-Up Pension Contributions deemed necessary to make up the Participant’s Pension Plan benefit if the Participant terminates employment prior to age 60. A Participant who terminates employment other than by reason of death or Disability prior to vesting in his Employer Contributions shall forfeit 100% of his Employer Contributions. All of a Participant’s Employer Contributions will fully vest upon the Participant’s death or Disability while actively employed by an Employer. A Participant will fully vest in his own Employee Contributions at all times. A Participant will fully vest in his Employer Special Contributions upon completion of five years of service. A Participant will fully vest in his Employer 10% Target Contributions as follows: less than 1 year of service – 0%, 1 year – 20%, 2 years – 40%, 3 years – 60%, 4 years – 80%, 5 or more years – 100%. Years of service used to determine vesting in Employer 10% Target Contributions is defined under the Savings Plan. A Participant will fully vest in his Employer Make-Up Matching Contributions and Employer Make-Up Pension Contributions upon the later of: (i) the Participant’s attainment of age 55, or (ii) the Participant’s completion of 5 years of service. A Participant terminated for cause shall forfeit 100% of the Participant’s Accounts. A Participant is terminated for cause when, in the sole discretion of the Committee, such Participant is terminated as a result of fraud, misappropriation, or embezzlement of Employer funds or property, or other misconduct as defined in the Plan. All Forfeitures shall be used to reduce Employer Contributions for the current Plan Year or succeeding Plan Years, or shall be used to pay reasonable administrative expenses of the Plan. The total amount, if any, of Salary Deferral Contributions, Bonus Contributions, Employer Make-Up Matching Contributions, Employer Make-Up Pension Contributions, and other Employer Contributions will be allocated to the Participant’s Accounts. A Participant shall have an interest or right in the Participant’s Accounts only as provided under the Plan. The Trust shall hold all assets of the Plan and shall consist of such investments or funds as the Investment Committee shall determine from time to time. Pending investment, reinvestment or distribution of assets, the Trustee may temporarily retain assets of any Investment Fund in cash, commercial paper, short-term obligations, or common or collective short-term investment funds. The Investment Committee may direct the Trustee to establish or terminate an Investment Fund as it shall from time to time consider appropriate. A Participant may elect to invest all or a portion of the Participant’s Account in one or more Investment Funds selected by the Investment Committee. A Participant also may elect to change or transfer the Participant’s Account balances to one or more other Investment Funds. All investment elections shall be made at the time and in the manner prescribed by the Investment Committee and shall be effective only at the Investment Committee’s discretion and as prescribed by the Investment Committee. A Participant will have the opportunity to make two separate investment elections: (i) one with respect to the Participant’s Employer Contributions, and (ii) one with respect to the Participant’s Employee Contributions. The Investment Committee shall determine whether expenses incurred in administering the Plan shall be paid from the Trust or by the Employers in such proportions and allocations as the Investment Committee determines. A Participant may elect the timing and form of payment for the Participant’s Grandfathered Accounts by completing a benefit election form prescribed by the Committee. A Participant may elect to receive the Participant’s Grandfathered Accounts as of: (i) the Participant’s termination of employment, or (ii) a specified date elected by the Participant. If a Participant terminates service from all Employers and their Affiliates prior to retirement, the Participant will receive a distribution of the Participant’s Grandfathered Accounts in a lump sum. The Committee shall determine if a Participant’s termination is due to retirement or Disability. Prior to the allocation of Employee Contributions to the Participant’s 409A Accounts, a Participant must elect the timing and form of payment for such Employee Contributions from the Participant’s 409A Accounts by completing a distribution election form in accordance with procedures prescribed by the Committee (the “Initial Election”). Beginning with contributions for 2007, a Participant shall make a separate distribution election for Employee Contributions in 409A Accounts. A Participant’s Employee Contributions in 409A Accounts will be treated as a single payment in accordance with the regulations under Section 409A of the Code. The Initial Election will apply to distributions of all Employee Contributions made prior to January 1, 2007, and applicable earnings or losses, in a Participant’s 409A Accounts unless the Participant executes another benefit election form (a “Second Election”), subject to the following provisions: (i) a Second Election will not take effect until twelve months after the date on which the Second Election is made, (ii) the payment date selected on a Second Election must be a date not less than five years from the date of the Participant’s termination of employment.

Beginning with contributions for 2007, a Participant must make a separate distribution election for Employee Contributions in their 409A Accounts, which will be treated as a single payment under Section 409A of the Code. The Initial Election applies to all Employee Contributions made prior to January 1, 2007, and any applicable earnings or losses in the Participant’s 409A Accounts, unless a Second Election is executed. A Second Election will not take effect until twelve months after it is made, and the payment date selected must be at least five years after the date of separation from service. Beginning January 1, 2007, Participants may modify their elections for 2005 and 2006 Employee Contributions regarding form and timing, but such modifications are subject to the same restrictions as Second Elections. For Employer Contributions, a Participant must elect either a lump sum or substantially equal annual installments over a two-year to ten-year period, with installment payments treated as a single payment under Section 409A regulations. Once an election is made, neither the Participant nor the Employer may change the timing or form of distribution. If no election is made, Employer Contributions are paid in a lump sum. A Participant may receive a hardship distribution due to an “Unforeseeable Financial Emergency,” defined as a sudden and unexpected illness or accident of the Participant or a dependent, loss of property due to casualty, or other similar extraordinary and unforeseeable circumstances beyond the Participant’s control. The amount of such distribution may be reduced if it is or may be relieved through insurance reimbursement, compensation, or liquidation of the Participant’s assets. If a Participant dies before receiving the full balance of their Accounts, the remaining balance becomes 100% vested and is paid to the designated Beneficiaries according to Committee procedures. If no Beneficiary designation exists, the balance is paid to the Participant’s estate. A Participant’s Beneficiary designation applies to all Accounts and may be changed at any time, with the most recent designation prior to death controlling. Payments to a Participant or Beneficiary under a legal disability or deemed unable to manage their affairs by the Committee are subject to the Plan’s facility of payment provisions. Participation in the Plan does not create any right, lien, or interest in the Employer’s assets; Participant Account balances remain unrestricted and are not subject to anticipation, alienation, sale, transfer, assignment, pledge, or encumbrance. All payments are made in cash from the general funds of the applicable Employer, with no special or segregated fund established. Employment taxes include the FICA tax under Sections 3101 and 3121(v)(2) of the Code on deferred compensation, the income tax on the FICA Amount under Section 3401, and any amounts attributable to such taxes. If the Company or Affiliate’s deduction for payment of benefits would be limited due to a failure to satisfy Section 409A, such payments may be permitted at the Company or Committee’s discretion under Treasury Regulations, IRS Notice 2005-1, Q&A-15, and any applicable subsequent guidance.

A Participant’s Beneficiary designation applies to all of their Accounts under the Plan, and the Participant may change such designations at any time; the most recent designation filed before the Participant’s death will govern. If no Beneficiary designation form has been submitted prior to the Participant’s death, the remaining Account balance will be paid to the Participant’s estate. The Plan provides for the payment of amounts to a Participant or Beneficiary who is under a legal disability or, in the Committee’s judgment, unable to manage their affairs. Participation in the Plan does not create any right, lien, or interest in the assets of any Employer, and a Participant’s Account balances remain the unrestricted assets of their Employer. A Participant’s rights to benefits are not subject to anticipation, alienation, sale, transfer, assignment, pledge, or encumbrance. All payments are made in cash from the general funds of the applicable Employer, with no special or separate fund established or assets segregated to ensure benefit payments. Nothing in the Plan or any action taken under it creates or is construed as creating a trust or a fiduciary relationship between any Employer and a Participant or any other person, and each Employer’s obligation to pay benefits remains unfunded. The Plan is administered by the Committee, which has the authority to interpret the Plan’s terms, resolve questions arising under it, adopt rules and regulations consistent with the Plan and Trust agreement, enforce the Plan, direct Trustees regarding payments or distributions, provide Employers with required information for tax or other purposes, and employ agents, attorneys, accountants, actuaries, or other persons to assist in administration, provided such appointments and delegations are in writing. The Investment Committee has full authority and control over the appointment of trustees and investment managers and the investment of Plan assets. Employers may deduct federal, state, or local taxes required by law from any payment under the Plan. For retirement claims related to Account determinations other than Disability, the Participant may appeal a denial within 60 days of receiving the initial denial notice, and may request a review by the Committee, with the right to submit a written appeal within 45 days of receiving the denial notice. If a claim is denied, the Participant may request a review by the Committee, and if the Committee determines that the claim is not properly addressed, the Participant may file a written request within 60 days of the initial denial. A Participant may appeal a denial of a claim related to their Account, and if the Committee determines that the claim is not properly addressed, the Participant may file a written request within 60 days of the initial denial. If a claim is denied, the Participant may request a review by the Committee, and if the Committee determines that the claim is not properly addressed, the Participant may file a written request within 60 days of the initial denial. The Committee’s determination, including any interpretation, rule, or administrative decision, is final and binding for all Plan purposes and upon all interested persons, their heirs, and their successors. The Committee may, at its discretion, provide, free of charge, copies of all documents, including those related to attorneys’ fees, that occur by reason of, arise out of, or are incidental to the implementation or administration of the Plan.

The Committee’s determinations, including any interpretations, rules, or administrative decisions, are final and binding for all Plan purposes and for all interested persons, their heirs, and personal representatives. No legal action to recover benefits under the Plan may be brought until the claim and review processes outlined in this Section have been exhausted and the requested benefits have been denied in whole or in part. If a judicial proceeding is initiated to appeal a claim denial or to bring any action under ERISA, except for a breach of fiduciary duty claim, the evidence presented must be limited to that which was timely submitted to the Committee. If the Committee denies a Participant’s appeal in whole or in part, and the Participant later files a claim against the Plan, any such legal action must be initiated within 120 days of the Committee’s final decision. Benefits are payable only if the Committee determines that a Participant or Beneficiary is entitled to them. The Plan does not confer any employment rights on participants, and the right of an Employer to dismiss or discharge any Participant is specifically reserved. In the event of a Change in Control—defined as the sale of stock or substantially all assets of an Employer, its subsidiary, or division, or a change in majority beneficial ownership—the Grandfathered Accounts of affected Participants become immediately due and payable unless a successor assumes the liabilities and responsibilities. Similarly, in the event of a Change in Control Event—defined under Code Section 409A and its regulations—such as a change in ownership, effective control, or ownership of a substantial portion of the Employer’s assets—the 409A Accounts of affected Participants become 100% vested and are immediately due and payable in a lump sum. The Board of Directors may amend, suspend, or terminate the Plan at any time by resolution, and may delegate such authority to the Committees or specified individuals. However, no amendment, modification, or termination may reduce a Participant’s vested Account balance without their consent. If the Plan is terminated, the Committee shall continue to administer it in accordance with its relevant provisions.
